title: Automatic iterative learning versus hypothesis-sized memory
formal: Does there exist an automatic language family learnable in the limit from positive texts with automatic hypothesis-length-bounded memory, but not learnable by any automatic iterative learner even after changing to another automatic hypothesis space?
definitions:
Fix finite data and index alphabets. The convolution of a finite tuple of strings is obtained by aligning their left ends and padding shorter strings on the right with a fresh symbol. A relation is automatic if a finite automaton recognizes its convolutions. An automatic language family has a regular index set I and an automatic membership relation {(i,x): x in L_i}. A learner may use any automatic hypothesis family {H_j:j in J} that includes every target language; duplicates, automatic recodings and hypotheses outside the target family are permitted.

A text for L is any infinite sequence of strings or a pause symbol # whose nonpause content is exactly L. Repetition and arbitrary ordering are allowed. A learner has a fixed initial memory and a total update map (m,x) to (m-prime,h-prime) with automatic graph, where memory is a string over a fixed finite alphabet, x is the next datum or pause and h-prime is a hypothesis index or the special no-conjecture symbol ?. Only m-prime is available at the next round; the output is not separate free storage. Success means that on every text for every target language, outputs eventually equal one fixed index j with H_j=L. Infinitely changing synonymous indices do not count as convergence. No negative counterexamples, queries about past data or extra tapes are available. Finite control is part of the fixed automaton. Bounds below hold on every finite data history, using maximum zero when no nonpause example has appeared.

Hypothesis-length-bounded means some constant c satisfies |m|≤|h|+c after every finite history; the special symbol ? has length one. An iterative learner stores exactly its current output hypothesis, including ?, as its entire persistent memory. Its next output and memory therefore depend only on that hypothesis and the new datum through an automatic function. The initial memory equals its initial hypothesis. Different learners may choose different automatic hypothesis families containing all targets. Padding an index with retained information is allowed if the resulting index family and membership relation remain automatic, but the padded index must eventually stabilize for successful learning.

An iterative learner is already hypothesis-length bounded, so the question asks whether this inclusion is strict. The separator must defeat every permitted iterative recoding, not only the indexing used by the more powerful learner.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked separating family, its bounded-memory learner and the impossibility proof against all iterative learners and recodings, or prove that every hypothesis-length-bounded automatic learner’s target family has an iterative automatic learner.
context: The distinction is not merely the number of stored bits: a separate bounded memory may keep changing after the visible hypothesis converges, while iterative storage is the converging hypothesis itself.
why: The comparison isolates the informational power of auxiliary memory in constrained learning models.

import_provenance.original_title: Automatic iterative learning versus hypothesis-sized memory
import_provenance.original_statement: Does allowing an automatic learner additional memory bounded by the length of its current hypothesis strictly increase what it can identify in the limit from positive data, compared with retaining only the previous hypothesis? Compare learnable automatic families allowing suitable automatic hypothesis-space recodings, rather than fixing a potentially restrictive original indexing.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: The question concerns positive examples without a counterexample oracle. The 2017 paper already proves iterative learning of automatic families consisting only of infinite languages when bounded negative counterexamples are supplied.

sentences: Both learner types use automatic updates and receive only positive texts.
One may keep a separate memory bounded by its hypothesis length.
The iterative learner retains only the hypothesis itself.
Both sides may choose padded or recoded automatic hypothesis spaces.
The question asks whether separate memory strictly increases learnability.
